parent: 分別禪波羅蜜前方便第六之二

zh: 第三、明修止方法，亦為三意：一、修繫緣止；二、修制心止；三、修體真止。第一、先明修繫緣止法者，略明有五處：一、繫心頂上；二、繫心髮際；三、繫心鼻柱；四、繫心臍間；五、繫心在地輪。外國金齒三藏說此為五門禪。問曰：身分皆可繫心，云何的說五處？答曰：此五處於用心為便，餘處非安定所。若脇、肋等處皆偏，故不說。如頭圓法天，足方法地，臍是氣海，鼻是風門，髮際是修骨觀之所，故以為門。
en: Third, clarifying the method of cultivating stopping: this too has three parts — cultivating fixed-object stopping; cultivating restraining-the-mind stopping; and cultivating embodying-truth stopping.

First, clarifying the method of cultivating fixed-object stopping: in brief, there are five places given — first, fixing the mind at the crown of the head; second, fixing the mind at the hairline; third, fixing the mind at the bridge of the nose; fourth, fixing the mind at the navel; fifth, fixing the mind at the ground-wheel, the base of the body. A foreign Tripiṭaka master named Kanacoṭi called this the five-gate dhyāna. Question: the mind can be fixed on any part of the body — why specify exactly these five places? Answer: these five places are especially convenient for applying the mind; other places are not proper seats of settling. Places such as the ribs and flanks are all uneven, and so are not spoken of. Just as the head, being round, corresponds to heaven, and the feet, being square, correspond to earth; the navel is the sea of vital energy; the nose is the gate of the breath; and the hairline is the place for cultivating the contemplation of bones — hence these are taken as the gates.

zh: 令繫心頂上者，為心沈惛多睡故，在上安心；若久久，即令人浮風，乍如風病，或似得通欲飛，有此等過，不可恒用。若繫心髮際，此處髮黑肉白，心則易住。或可發本骨觀，久則過生，眼好上瞻，或可見於黃、赤等色，如華如雲，種種相貌，令情慮顛倒。若繫心鼻柱者，鼻是風門，覺出息、入息，念念不住，易悟無常。亦以扶本安般之習，心靜能發禪定。若繫心臍下，臍是氣海，亦曰中宮，繫心在臍，能除眾病，或時內見三十六物，發特勝等禪。若繫心地輪，此最在下，氣隨心下，則四大調和。亦以扶本修習不淨觀者，多從下起，因此繫心，或能發本。不淨觀門約此五處為緣，令心不散，以辨修繫緣止，意在於此。
en: As for fixing the mind at the crown of the head: this is done because, when the mind is sunken and dull, prone to drowsiness, settling it above helps counter this; but if done for too long, it can cause a person to become light-headed, resembling wind-illness, or make them feel as though they have gained the power to fly — such faults as these mean it should not be used constantly. As for fixing the mind at the hairline: since the hair here is dark and the flesh pale, the mind settles here easily; it may also bring forth the underlying contemplation of bones — but if done too long, faults arise: the eyes tend to gaze upward, or one may see yellow, red, and other colors, like flowers or clouds, various such appearances, causing the feelings and deliberations to become inverted. As for fixing the mind at the bridge of the nose: the nose is the gate of the breath, and, being aware of the breath going out and coming in, moment by moment never remaining still, impermanence is easily realized; this also builds upon the underlying practice of mindfulness of the breath, and, the mind becoming still, dhyāna-concentration can be brought forth. As for fixing the mind below the navel: the navel is the sea of vital energy, also called the central palace; fixing the mind at the navel is able to remove many illnesses, and one may, at times, inwardly see the thirty-six impure substances of the body, bringing forth the special-excellences dhyāna and the like. As for fixing the mind at the ground-wheel: this is the lowest of all, and, the vital energy following the mind downward, the four elements become harmonized; this also builds upon the habituation of those who have cultivated the contemplation of impurity, which for the most part arises from below — fixing the mind here may bring forth the underlying gate of the contemplation of impurity. Taking these five places as objects, so that the mind does not scatter — the intent behind distinguishing the cultivation of fixed-object stopping lies exactly here.

zh: 譬如猨猴得樹，騰躍跳躑，若鎖之於柱，久久自調。心亦如是，若心停住，未入定前復有一止，名凝心止。若得入定，身心泯然，任運自寂，即是入定止。二、明修制心止者，心非形色，亦無處所，豈可繫之在境？但是妄想緣慮，故須制之。心若靜住，則不須制之，但凝其心，息諸亂想，即是修止。問曰：心非上下，有時若寬若急，若沈浮，調適之法，其事云何？答曰：心雖非上下，為治沈浮患故，上下安之，於行無失。若心浮動，可作意下著止之；若心沈沒，可上著止之。復次，若下著安心，利益眾多，略說有二：一、心易得定；二者、眾病不生。
en: It is like a monkey that, finding a tree, leaps and bounds about — but if chained to a post, it will, in time, settle down of itself. The mind is exactly the same: once the mind comes to rest, but before entering concentration proper, there is a further kind of stopping, called congealed-mind stopping. Once concentration is actually attained, body and mind dissolve away, and stillness arises spontaneously of itself — this is stopping that has entered concentration.

Second, clarifying the cultivation of restraining-the-mind stopping: the mind has no shape or form, nor any location — how could it truly be fixed upon an object at all? It is only deluded thought and deliberation that must be restrained. If the mind is already settled and still, there is no need to restrain it further — one need only let the mind congeal, bringing every scattered thought to rest, and this is cultivating stopping.

Question: the mind has no up or down — yet at times it becomes too slack or too tense, or sinks or floats; what, then, is the method for adjusting it properly? Answer: though the mind truly has no up or down, in order to treat the troubles of sinking and floating, settling it lower or higher can be applied without fault to the practice. If the mind is floating and agitated, one may direct the intention downward to settle and still it; if the mind is sinking, one may direct it upward to settle and still it. Furthermore, settling the mind lower brings many benefits; in brief, two may be given: first, concentration is more easily attained; second, the many illnesses do not arise.

The five points for fixed-object stopping are worth comparing with fascicle 1's earlier note on the kalala stage of conception: the same instinct to ground abstract practice in concrete physiology recurs here, down to specific cautions about side effects (light-headedness from too much attention at the crown; from too much at the hairline, eyes that tend to gaze upward and visions of colors that turn the feelings and deliberations upside down). The monkey-and-post simile is a classical image for the untrained mind that recurs throughout later Buddhist meditation literature.

items.en: Embodying-Truth Stopping: Is There Any Karma to Be Found?
items.zh: 明修止方法 · 修體真止
parent: 分別禪波羅蜜前方便第六之二

zh: 第三、明修體真止者，以正智慧體一切陰入界、三毒、九十八使及十二因緣等三界因果諸法悉皆空寂，如《大品經》中說：「即色是空，非色滅空，色性自空。空即是色，色即是空。離色無空，離空無色。受、想、行、識等一切諸法亦皆如是。」所以者何？今現見陰入界等諸法自性不有，何能生我、人、眾生、壽命等一切諸顛倒事？
en: Third, clarifying the cultivation of embodying-truth stopping: by means of right wisdom, one embodies the fact that every dharma of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, the three poisons, the ninety-eight fetters, the twelve links of dependent origination, and every cause and result within the three realms, is, without exception, empty and still — as the Larger Sūtra says: "Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases and thereby becomes emptiness — form's very nature is, of itself, empty. Emptiness is itself form, and form is itself emptiness. Apart from form there is no emptiness, and apart from emptiness there is no form. Sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness — every dharma whatsoever — are all exactly the same." Why is this? Now, actually observing that the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and every other such dharma have no self-nature of their own — how could they possibly give rise to a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, or any of the other inverted notions?

zh: 云何知空？如過去所起一切煩惱業行為因，現在攬父母身分為緣，因緣和合則有果報；有果報故，則有陰入界等一切諸法者，此業為是何法，而能為果報、陰入等作因？若言過去善心即是業者，過去作善之心及心數法皆已滅謝，豈得為現在果報及陰入等法作因？若言心非是業因，心作業，業隨心來者，心轉滅故，業亦應隨心轉滅。若業轉滅，豈能感今世果報及陰入等法？若業轉滅，當知業即不至現在。何以故？業不來故。若業不來而受報者，此報不名報。何以故？無業則報無所酬。
en: How is emptiness to be known? Suppose it is said: the afflictions and karmic actions arisen in the past serve as cause, and the present taking hold of a body from one's parents serves as condition; when cause and condition come together, a result is thereby produced, and because there is a result, all the dharmas of the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and the rest come to exist. If this is so — what kind of thing, exactly, is this karma, that it is able to serve as the cause of the result, the aggregates, and the rest?

If it is said that the wholesome mind of the past is itself the karma: the mind, and the mental factors that performed that good deed in the past, have already ceased and passed away — how, then, could they still serve as the cause of the present result, the aggregates, and the rest? If it is said that the mind is not the karmic cause, but rather that the mind produces karma, and the karma then follows along with the mind: since the mind ceases and changes, the karma too ought to cease and change along with it. And if the karma has already ceased and changed, how could it possibly bring about the present result, the aggregates, and the rest? If the karma has already ceased and changed, it should be known that this karma simply does not reach into the present at all. Why is this? Because the karma itself does not arrive here. And if a result is received without the karma itself ever arriving, this so-called result cannot properly be called a result at all — why is this? Because, without the karma, there is nothing for the result to answer to.

zh: 若言過去心雖滅謝，而次心續生，故業得隨心來者，亦應過去業雖滅謝，次業續生，故得至現在。若爾，即有大失。何以故？或時過去善心滅而惡心續生，今亦應過去善業滅而次惡業續生，此唯見惡業至現在。若爾，應感惡報，何得感善果耶？若言業來而不隨心者，此業應自有報，離心而受。今實不爾。復次，業若有相，即是有為；若是有為，必墮三相。若墮三相；即是生滅；若是生滅，即不至現在。過去既滅，當知本業亦滅，誰感此果？不可以新業始生，能感今果。當知業有相貌，此義不可。若言業無相貌而能感果者，此亦不然。所以者何？無相之法，即是無為。無為無業，何得感果？復次，無相之法即是空義，空無生滅，豈得名業？若說空無相能感果者，三無為法亦應感果。既不得爾，云何而言業是無相而能感果？如是種種因緣，業不可得，當知無有此業。
en: If it is said that, although the past mind has ceased and passed away, a subsequent mind arises in succession, and so the karma is able to follow along and arrive with this subsequent mind — then it ought equally to be said that, although the past karma has ceased and passed away, a subsequent karma arises in succession, and so it is able to reach into the present. But if this is so, a great fault follows. Why is this? At times the past wholesome mind ceases and an unwholesome mind arises in succession after it — and, by the same logic, the past wholesome karma ought then to cease and an unwholesome karma arise in succession after it, so that only unwholesome karma would ever be seen reaching into the present. If this is so, only unwholesome retribution ought to be received — how, then, could any wholesome fruit ever be obtained? If it is said that the karma arrives without following along with the mind at all, then this karma ought to have its own result entirely apart from the mind, received independently of it — but this is, in fact, not so.

Furthermore: if karma has a mark or characteristic, it is a conditioned dharma; and if it is conditioned, it must fall under the three marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing. And if it falls under these three marks, it is subject to arising and ceasing; and if it is subject to arising and ceasing, it cannot reach into the present at all. Since the past has already ceased, the original karma must likewise have ceased — so who, then, brings about this present result? It cannot be that karma newly arisen now is able to bring about the present result instead. One should know, then, that the notion of karma possessing a fixed mark or characteristic is untenable.

If it is said instead that karma, having no mark or characteristic, is nonetheless able to bring about a result — this too does not hold. Why is this? A dharma without any mark whatsoever is precisely an unconditioned dharma; and an unconditioned dharma has no karma in it at all — how, then, could it bring about a result? Furthermore, a dharma without any mark is precisely what is meant by emptiness itself; emptiness has no arising and ceasing — how, then, could it be called karma at all? And if it is said that emptiness, being without mark, is able to bring about a result, then the three unconditioned dharmas ought equally to be able to bring about a result — and since this cannot be so, how can it still be said that karma, being without mark, is able to bring about a result? Through causes and conditions such as these, karma can, in the end, never be found — one should know, then, that there is, in truth, no such thing as this karma at all.

zh: 若業不可得，云何言陰入界等一切皆從內業因生？亦不從外緣生者，若定從緣而有報者，則一切陰陽會時，皆應有果報、陰入界等一切諸法。若爾，則不待業持識來，方乃有生，故知非外緣生。若謂因緣合，故有果報、陰入等法生者，若因緣中各有生，合時應有二生；若各無生，合時何得而有生？若謂離因緣而有生者，此事不然。從因緣故有生尚不可，何況無因緣而有生？若無因緣而有生者，則因果義壞。世間行善之人應得惡報，行惡之人應得善報，亦不應有修道，此即破於世間善惡因果，名大邪見。當知陰入等一切諸法不從內因有，亦不從外緣有，亦不因緣合故有，亦不無因緣有。若非有，即是空。若於無所有空中計有者，當知但是無明顛倒妄計為有。
en: If karma cannot be found at all, how can it still be said that the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and the rest all arise from an internal karmic cause? Nor do they arise from an external condition alone: if a result definitely arose merely from external conditions, then whenever any two things of yin and yang came together, a result, and the aggregates and the rest, ought to arise there as well. But if this were so, there would be no need to wait for karma sustaining consciousness to arrive before birth could occur at all — hence it is known that this does not arise from external condition alone either. If it is said that cause and condition come together, and therefore the result, the aggregates, and the rest arise: if each of cause and condition already contains arising within itself, then, when they come together, there ought to be two arisings; but if neither contains arising at all, how could arising possibly occur once they come together? And if it is said that arising occurs apart from both cause and condition, this too does not hold — for if arising through cause and condition is already untenable, how much more untenable is arising with no cause or condition whatsoever? If there could be arising with no cause or condition at all, the very meaning of cause and effect would collapse: those in the world who do good ought then to receive evil retribution, and those who do evil ought to receive good retribution, and there would be no reason for anyone to cultivate the path at all — this would utterly destroy the world's own principle of good and evil, cause and effect, and is called a great wrong view.

One should know, then, that the aggregates, sense-bases, and every other such dharma do not exist from an internal cause alone, nor from an external condition alone, nor from cause and condition coming together, nor without any cause or condition at all. If they are not truly existent in any of these ways, they are empty. And if, within this very emptiness where nothing at all exists, existence is still conceived, one should know that this is nothing but ignorance and inverted thinking, falsely conceiving existence where there is none.

zh:
若了知顛倒所計之法一切悉皆虛誑，猶如夢幻，但有名字，名字之法亦不可得，則言語道斷，心行處滅，畢竟空寂，猶如虛空。若行者體知一切諸法如虛空者，無取無捨，無依無倚，無住無著。若心無取捨、依倚、住著，則一切妄想顛倒生死業行悉皆止息，無為無欲，無念無行，無造無作，無示無說，無諍無競，泯然清淨，如大涅槃，是名真止。此則止無所止，無止之止，名體真止。故經偈云：
一切諸法中，因緣空無主，
息心達本源，故號為沙門。
en: If one comes to understand clearly that everything conceived through such inverted thinking is, in every case, illusory and unreal, just like a dream or a magical apparition — possessing only a name, and even that name-dharma being itself unfindable — then the path of language is cut off, the sphere of mental activity is extinguished, and all is, in the end, empty and still, just like empty space itself.

If a practitioner embodies the knowledge that all dharmas are like empty space, there is nothing to grasp and nothing to reject, nothing to depend on and nothing to lean against, nothing to abide in and nothing to cling to. And if the mind is free of grasping and rejecting, depending and leaning, abiding and clinging, then every deluded thought, every inverted notion, every karmic action of birth-and-death is thereby brought entirely to rest — unconditioned, free of desire, free of thought, free of activity, free of fabrication and construction, free of display and of speech, free of contention and of striving, dissolved away into purity, like great nirvāṇa itself. This is what is called true stopping. This, then, is a stopping that stops nothing, a stopping with nothing left to stop — this is what is called embodying-truth stopping. Hence the sūtra says in verse:
"Within all dharmas whatsoever, causes and conditions are empty, with no master over them;
Stilling the mind, one reaches the very source — hence one is called a śramaṇa."

This is the treatise's third sustained tetralemma-style analysis (after fascicle 1's against "contaminated dharma" and fascicle 2's against "offense"), now aimed at karma itself: can it be found in the wholesome mind that produced it, in a mind-independent transmission, in a fixed characteristic, or in the total absence of one? None survive scrutiny. Note carefully what the passage does not conclude — it never says karma and its results are unreal or that ethical cause-and-effect can be dismissed; it explicitly names the opposite conclusion ("those who do good ought to receive evil retribution... this is a great wrong view") as the actual danger of getting this analysis wrong. The point is that karma has no fixed, independently findable essence, not that it doesn't function conventionally. This is "embodying-truth stopping" in full: not a technique applied to the mind from outside, but the mind's own direct realization of emptiness, described here as identical with the language used elsewhere for nirvāṇa itself. This closes the third of the gate of stopping's four parts.

quiz.q: Fixed-object stopping is cultivated at five places. Which?
options: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body
crown, hairline, bridge of the nose, navel, ground-wheel
crown, brow, throat, heart, navel
hands, feet, flanks, ribs, back
quiz.why: "First, fixing the mind at the crown of the head; second, fixing the mind at the hairline; third, fixing the mind at the bridge of the nose; fourth, fixing the mind at the navel; fifth, fixing the mind at the ground-wheel." Places such as the ribs and flanks are uneven and not spoken of.

quiz.q: Which matches the text's reason for taking these five places as gates?
options: the round head corresponds to heaven, the square feet to earth, the navel is the sea of vital energy, the nose the gate of the breath, the hairline the place for contemplating bones
they are five of the Buddha's marks
they correspond to the five organs
they correspond to the five hindrances
quiz.why: "These five places are especially convenient for applying the mind ... Just as the head, being round, corresponds to heaven, and the feet, being square, correspond to earth; the navel is the sea of vital energy; the nose is the gate of the breath; and the hairline is the place for cultivating the contemplation of bones."

quiz.q: What is fixing the mind at the crown of the head meant to treat, and what fault comes from using it too long?
options: for a sunken, drowsy mind; too long, it causes light-headedness like wind-illness or a feeling of being able to fly
to realize impermanence; too long shows the thirty-six substances
for agitation; too long causes dullness
to cure illness; no fault
quiz.why: "Fixing the mind at the crown of the head: this is done because, when the mind is sunken and dull, prone to drowsiness, settling it above helps counter this; but if done for too long, it can cause a person to become light-headed, resembling wind-illness, or make them feel as though they have gained the power to fly." Impermanence belongs to the nose and curing illness to the navel.

quiz.q: What benefit does fixing the mind at the bridge of the nose bring?
options: dark hair and pale skin make the mind settle
cures illness and reveals the thirty-six substances
the nose is the gate of the breath; aware of the breath moment by moment, impermanence is easily realized; it also builds on prior breath practice
harmonizes the elements and brings forth impurity contemplation
quiz.why: "The nose is the gate of the breath, and, being aware of the breath going out and coming in, moment by moment never remaining still, impermanence is easily realized; this also builds upon the underlying practice of mindfulness of the breath." The others describe the navel, the ground-wheel, and the hairline.

quiz.q: What simile illustrates fixed-object stopping, and what is the stopping just before entering concentration called?
options: still water; true-nature stopping
an ox driving a wheel; embodying-truth stopping
taming a horse; entered-concentration stopping
a monkey leaping in a tree, chained to a post until it settles; fixed-mind stopping
quiz.why: "It is like a monkey that, finding a tree, leaps and bounds about — but if chained to a post, it will, in time, settle down of itself. The mind is exactly the same: once the mind comes to rest, but before entering concentration proper, there is a further kind of stopping, called fixed-mind stopping."

quiz.q: In examining karma under embodying-truth stopping, how does the text refute the claim that karma follows along with the mind?
options: since the mind ceases, karma should cease with it; if it ceased, it never reaches the present, so how could it bring the present result?
karma is unconditioned and so produces results
karma does follow the mind, hence results
karma arises from external conditions
quiz.why: "If it is said that ... the mind produces the karma, and the karma then follows along with the mind: since the mind ceases and changes, the karma too ought to cease and change along with it. And if the karma has already ceased and changed, how could it possibly bring about the present result?" The text also refutes the idea that markless karma produces results.

quiz.q: What fault follows if arising occurs apart from cause and condition?
options: the meaning of cause and effect collapses — good would bring evil and evil good, there would be no reason to cultivate, and this is a great wrong view
it would become unconditioned
two results would arise
no fault
quiz.why: "If there could be arising with no cause or condition at all, the very meaning of cause and effect would collapse: those in the world who do good ought then to receive evil retribution ... and there would be no reason for anyone to cultivate the path at all ... and is called a great wrong view." Two arisings is the fault of cause and condition each containing arising.

quiz.q: The verse ending the section on embodying-truth stopping begins, "Within all dharmas, causes and conditions are empty, with no master." How does it continue?
options: restrain it to one place and nothing is left undone
offenses are like frost, which the sun of wisdom dissolves
beings are attached everywhere; lead them out
stilling the mind, one reaches the very source — hence one is called a śramaṇa
quiz.why: The verse: "Within all dharmas whatsoever, causes and conditions are empty, with no master over them; / Stilling the mind, one reaches the very source — hence one is called a śramaṇa."
